title: Tukaram
carry: one for you and one for me

segments.voice: Yesterday: Namdev chased a dog with the butter, and sang behind a temple until, the story says, it turned to face him.

A man walks home along a village road with an armful of sugarcane, a gift from a farmer whose field he'd been helping with. You peel it and chew it for the sweet juice. Children see him coming and run up. Can we have some? He hands one stalk to the first child. Then the next, and the next. By the time he reaches his own door, he's holding a single stalk. Waiting inside is his wife, with a household to feed. The man is Tukaram.
screen: `AN ARMFUL OF SUGARCANE.` → `THE CHILDREN ASK.` → `ONE STALK LEFT.`

segments.voice: Tukaram is remembered as a grocer in the village of Dehu, on the Indrayani river, a devotee of Vitthal, the same god Namdev sang to. Tradition ties the two together: it says Namdev came to Tukaram in a dream, with Vitthal beside him, and set him the task of making songs. And the songs came. The stories don't pretend his life was easy. Tradition says his shop failed, famine hit his region, and he lost people he loved. Out of that grief, the stories say, he turned his whole life toward Vitthal. Back to the door, and the one stalk. His wife is furious. Tradition remembers her as sharp-tongued, but the story is fair to her: the family is poor, and her husband keeps giving everything away. She grabs the last stalk and brings it down across his back. It snaps in two. And Tukaram, rubbing his shoulder, looks at the pieces and says something like: wonderful, now there's one for you and one for me. It's funny. It's also a man who has decided, all the way down, that nothing he's handed is his to hoard, not the cane, not even the moment of being hit. The anger doesn't get a fight back. It gets half the sugarcane. His Varkari tradition doesn't ask anyone to leave home for a cave. It holds up people like this: a grocer, a husband, with debts and a hungry household at the door, singing to Vitthal right in the middle of it.
screen: `A GROCER OF DEHU.` · `NAMDEV IN A DREAM.` · `THE STALK SNAPS IN TWO.` · then, large: `ONE FOR YOU AND ONE FOR ME.`

segments.voice: Let your shoulders drop, and think of something you were handed lately, time, money, patience, that you gave away along the road before it reached the people at home. Don't scold yourself or defend yourself; just notice where it went, and who is waiting at your own door. If you pray, you can hold both the road and the door before God.
Tukaram. The grocer-saint of Dehu who gave away the sugarcane on the road home, and split the last broken stalk with the wife who broke it.
Your line: one for you and one for me. Even a broken stalk can be shared. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Tukaram belongs to the Varkari tradition of Maharashtra; Varkaris sing his songs to Vitthal at home and in temples, and the stories of his life are told and retold among them.
